questions.q: Why must food be digested?
choices: so the body can make more enzymes
so food can be passed out as faeces
so food can be stored in the stomach
so nutrients can be absorbed into the blood
questions.explain: Most food is made of large molecules that cannot pass into the blood. Digestion breaks them into small, soluble molecules so the nutrients can be absorbed into the blood.
questions.lo: Explain the importance of the digestive system (food must become small soluble molecules)

notes.0: Enzymes are made by the body's cells, not from digested food. Think about what has to happen to nutrients before the body can use them.
notes.1: Faeces is mostly the undigested part of food. Digestion is about the part of food the body can take in and use.
notes.2: The stomach holds food only for a short time. Digestion is about getting nutrients into a form the body can take in.

why.right: Food must be digested because large food molecules are too big to pass through the gut wall into the blood.
wrong: Food must be digested because large food molecules are too heavy to be pushed along the gut.
Food must be digested because large food molecules would be absorbed too quickly into the blood.

questions.q: The end products of digestion are
questions.explain: Digestion breaks large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules. Only small, soluble molecules can pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.
questions.lo: Explain the importance of the digestive system (food must become small soluble molecules)

notes.1: Large, insoluble molecules are what food starts as, before digestion. Think about what form the molecules need to pass into the blood.
notes.2: Small size is right, but insoluble molecules cannot dissolve in blood or pass through the gut wall. Think about whether they must dissolve.
notes.3: Large molecules cannot pass through the gut wall even if they dissolve. Think about what size the molecules need to be.

why.right: Digested food molecules must be small and soluble so they can pass through the gut wall into the blood.
wrong: Digested food molecules must be small and soluble so they can be stored in the stomach for later.
Digested food molecules must be small and soluble so they can be passed out quickly as faeces.

questions.q: An amoeba has no digestive system. How does it get nutrients?
choices: it makes them with lipases only
it chews food into small pieces
it absorbs them from its surroundings
it digests food in a stomach
questions.explain: An amoeba is a single cell. It takes in nutrients directly from the water around it through its cell surface, so it does not need a digestive system.
questions.lo: Explain the importance of the digestive system (food must become small soluble molecules)

notes.0: Lipases are enzymes that digest fats. They do not make nutrients. Think about how a single cell can take in substances from the water around it.
notes.1: Chewing needs teeth and a mouth, which an amoeba does not have. Think about how a single cell can take in substances from the water around it.
notes.3: An amoeba has no digestive system, so it has no stomach. Think about how a single cell can take in substances from the water around it.

why.right: An amoeba can take in nutrients directly because it is a single cell surrounded by water.
wrong: An amoeba can take in nutrients directly because it makes all its nutrients from water.
An amoeba can take in nutrients directly because it has a small stomach inside its cell.

questions.q: Rice is rich in which nutrient?
questions.explain: Rice is rich in starch. Starch is a carbohydrate, so rice is rich in carbohydrates.
questions.lo: Identify foods rich in carbohydrates, proteins and fats

notes.0: Proteins are found mainly in meat, fish, eggs and tofu. Rice is a starchy food, so think about which nutrient group starch belongs to.
notes.2: Fats are found mainly in butter, oil and nuts. Rice is a starchy food, so think about which nutrient group starch belongs to.
notes.3: Rice has only a little fibre, especially white rice. Rice is a starchy food, so think about which nutrient group starch belongs to.

questions.q: Butter is rich in which nutrient?
questions.explain: Butter is made from the fat in cream, so it is rich in fats.
questions.lo: Identify foods rich in carbohydrates, proteins and fats

notes.1: Carbohydrates are found mainly in rice, bread and potatoes. Butter is made from cream and feels greasy, so think about which nutrient that suggests.
notes.2: Fibre comes from plant foods such as vegetables and fruit. Butter comes from milk, so it has no fibre.
notes.3: Butter has only a little protein. It is made from cream and feels greasy, so think about which nutrient that suggests.

questions.q: A meal of avocado, peanuts and full cream milk is richest in
questions.explain: Avocado, peanuts and full cream milk all contain a lot of fat. So the meal is richest in fats.
questions.lo: Identify foods rich in carbohydrates, proteins and fats

notes.0: Carbohydrate-rich foods are things like rice, bread and noodles. Avocado, peanuts and full cream milk all contain a lot of an oily nutrient.
notes.1: Peanuts and milk do contain some protein, but all three foods share a larger amount of another nutrient. Think about what makes milk full cream.
notes.2: Avocado and peanuts have some fibre, but milk has none. Look for the nutrient that all three foods contain a lot of.

questions.q: A student wants a snack rich in proteins. Which should she choose?
questions.explain: Tofu is made from soya beans and is rich in proteins. Potatoes and biscuits are rich in carbohydrates, and cooking oil is fat.
questions.lo: Identify foods rich in carbohydrates, proteins and fats

notes.0: Potatoes are rich in starch, which is a carbohydrate. Think about foods that come from beans, meat, fish or eggs.
notes.1: Biscuits are made mostly of flour and sugar, which are carbohydrates. Think about foods that come from beans, meat, fish or eggs.
notes.3: Cooking oil is almost pure fat. Think about foods that come from beans, meat, fish or eggs.

questions.q: Physical digestion breaks food down by
questions.explain: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces by crushing, grinding and mixing. It increases the surface area for enzymes but does not change the food molecules.
questions.lo: Classify a process as physical or chemical digestion

notes.0: Killing microorganisms is done by the acid in the stomach. It does not break food into smaller pieces.
notes.2: The action of enzymes is chemical digestion. Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces without changing the molecules.
notes.3: Absorption happens after digestion, when nutrients pass into the blood. Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces without changing the molecules.

questions.q: Chemical digestion breaks food down by
questions.explain: Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large food molecules into small, soluble molecules.
questions.lo: Classify a process as physical or chemical digestion

notes.0: Chewing with the teeth is physical digestion. Chemical digestion changes the food molecules themselves.
notes.2: Mucus softens and lubricates food. It does not break food molecules down. Chemical digestion changes the food molecules themselves.
notes.3: Churning in the stomach is physical digestion. Chemical digestion changes the food molecules themselves.

questions.q: Teeth crush a piece of bread. Which process is this?
questions.explain: Crushing bread with the teeth breaks it into smaller pieces without changing its molecules. This is physical digestion.
questions.lo: Classify a process as physical or chemical digestion

notes.1: Chemical digestion needs enzymes to break molecules apart. Teeth only break the bread into smaller pieces.
notes.2: Absorption is when digested nutrients pass into the blood. Crushing bread happens in the mouth, long before that.

why.right: Crushing by teeth is physical digestion because it breaks food into smaller pieces without changing its molecules.
wrong: Crushing by teeth is physical digestion because the teeth release enzymes that break down the molecules.
Crushing by teeth is physical digestion because the crushed food passes straight into the blood.

questions.q: Proteases break down protein in a piece of fish. Which process is this?
questions.explain: Proteases are enzymes. They break protein molecules into amino acids, so this is chemical digestion.
questions.lo: Classify a process as physical or chemical digestion

notes.0: Physical digestion only breaks food into smaller pieces. Proteases are enzymes that change the protein molecules themselves.
notes.1: Absorption is when small nutrients pass into the blood. Proteases are enzymes that break down protein molecules first.

why.right: Protein breakdown by proteases is chemical digestion because enzymes change the protein into smaller molecules.
wrong: Protein breakdown by proteases is chemical digestion because proteases grind the fish into small pieces.
Protein breakdown by proteases is chemical digestion because proteases carry the fish into the blood.

questions.q: The stomach churns a meal into smaller pieces. Which process is this?
questions.explain: Churning by the stomach muscles breaks the meal into smaller pieces and mixes it. The food molecules are not changed, so this is physical digestion.
questions.lo: Classify a process as physical or chemical digestion

notes.0: Absorption is when nutrients pass into the blood. Churning only breaks food into smaller pieces.
notes.1: Chemical digestion needs enzymes to change food molecules. Churning by muscles only breaks food into smaller pieces.

why.right: Churning in the stomach is physical digestion because muscles break food into pieces without changing its molecules.
wrong: Churning in the stomach is physical digestion because the muscles release enzymes that break down molecules.
Churning in the stomach is physical digestion because the acid turns the food into new substances.

questions.q: Which organ carries out chemical digestion but no physical digestion?
questions.explain: In the small intestine, enzymes complete the chemical digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats. The mouth and stomach carry out both physical and chemical digestion.
questions.lo: Classify a process as physical or chemical digestion

notes.0: The rectum only stores faeces. No digestion of any kind happens there.
notes.1: The stomach carries out both. Its muscles churn food, which is physical digestion, and its gastric juice contains enzymes.
notes.2: The mouth carries out both. Teeth crush food, which is physical digestion, and saliva contains enzymes.

why.right: The small intestine digests food only chemically because its enzymes act on food that has already been broken up.
wrong: The small intestine digests food only chemically because its folds grind the food into tiny pieces.
The small intestine digests food only chemically because its acid kills the microorganisms in the food.

questions.q: Enzymes in the digestive system
choices: speed up the breakdown of large food molecules
absorb digested food into the blood
slow down the breakdown of food
questions.explain: Digestive enzymes speed up the breakdown of large food molecules into small, soluble molecules.
questions.lo: State the role of enzymes and that they are specific

notes.1: Absorption is done by the wall of the small intestine, not by enzymes. Think about what enzymes do to large food molecules.
notes.2: Food is pushed along the gullet by its muscles, not by enzymes. Think about what enzymes do to large food molecules.
notes.3: Enzymes make reactions faster, not slower. Think about how quickly food would break down without them.

questions.q: Enzymes are specific. This means each enzyme
choices: acts on only one type of substance
acts on every type of food
questions.explain: An enzyme is specific. It acts on only one type of substance. For example, proteases act on proteins but not on starch or fats.
questions.lo: State the role of enzymes and that they are specific

notes.0: Being specific is not about where an enzyme works. Enzymes act in the mouth, stomach and small intestine. Think about which substances each enzyme acts on.
notes.2: If an enzyme acted on every type of food, it would not be specific. Think about why the body needs several different enzymes.
notes.3: Digestive enzymes break food molecules into smaller ones, not larger ones. Being specific is about which substances an enzyme acts on.

questions.q: Lipases are added to a mixture of starch and protein. What happens?
choices: only the protein is broken down
only the starch is broken down
questions.explain: Lipases are specific to fats. The mixture contains only starch and protein, so the lipases cannot break down either of them.
questions.lo: State the role of enzymes and that they are specific

notes.0: Proteins are broken down by proteases, not lipases. Each enzyme acts on only one type of substance.
notes.1: Starch is broken down by carbohydrases, not lipases. Each enzyme acts on only one type of substance.
notes.2: Lipases cannot act on every food. Each enzyme acts on only one type of substance, so check what lipases act on.

why.right: Lipases leave starch and protein unchanged because each enzyme acts on only one type of substance.
wrong: Lipases leave starch and protein unchanged because lipases only work inside the mouth.
Lipases leave starch and protein unchanged because lipases are used up before they can act.

questions.q: Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates into
questions.explain: Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates such as starch into simple sugars.
questions.lo: Match each enzyme class to its food and end product

notes.0: Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats, broken down by lipases. Think about the small units that carbohydrates are made of.
notes.1: Digestion makes molecules smaller and does not turn one nutrient into another. Think about the small units that carbohydrates are made of.
notes.3: Amino acids come from proteins, broken down by proteases. Think about the small units that carbohydrates are made of.

questions.q: Proteases break down proteins into
questions.explain: Proteases break down proteins into amino acids.
questions.lo: Match each enzyme class to its food and end product

notes.1: Starch is a carbohydrate, not a product of protein digestion. Think about the small units that proteins are made of.
notes.2: Simple sugars come from carbohydrates, broken down by carbohydrases. Think about the small units that proteins are made of.
notes.3: Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats, broken down by lipases. Think about the small units that proteins are made of.

questions.q: Lipases break down fats into
questions.explain: Lipases break down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
questions.lo: Match each enzyme class to its food and end product

notes.0: Amino acids come from proteins, broken down by proteases. Think about the small units that fats are made of.
notes.2: Digestion makes molecules smaller and does not turn fats into proteins. Think about the small units that fats are made of.
notes.3: Simple sugars come from carbohydrates, broken down by carbohydrases. Think about the small units that fats are made of.

questions.q: Digestion of a food produces amino acids. Which enzymes acted?
questions.explain: Amino acids are the end products of protein digestion. Proteins are broken down by proteases.
questions.lo: Match each enzyme class to its food and end product

notes.0: Lipases break down fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Think about which nutrient is made of amino acids.
notes.2: Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates into simple sugars. Think about which nutrient is made of amino acids.

why.right: Amino acids show protease action because proteases are the enzymes that break proteins into amino acids.
wrong: Amino acids show protease action because proteases break fats into amino acids and glycerol.
Amino acids show protease action because proteases join simple sugars together into amino acids.

questions.q: Digestion of a food produces fatty acids and glycerol. Which food was it?
questions.explain: Fatty acids and glycerol are the end products of fat digestion by lipases. So the food was fats.
questions.lo: Match each enzyme class to its food and end product

notes.0: Carbohydrates are digested into simple sugars. Think about which nutrient is broken into fatty acids and glycerol.
notes.1: Proteins are digested into amino acids. Think about which nutrient is broken into fatty acids and glycerol.
notes.2: Fibre is not digested in the human gut, so it produces no end products. Think about which nutrient lipases act on.

why.right: Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats because lipases break each fat molecule into these smaller units.
wrong: Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats because fats are digested into amino acids first.
Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats because proteases break each fat molecule into these smaller units.

questions.q: Which enzymes are needed to fully digest the starch in bread?
questions.explain: Starch is a carbohydrate. Carbohydrases break starch down into simple sugars.
questions.lo: Match each enzyme class to its food and end product

notes.0: Lipases act only on fats. Starch is a different nutrient, so think about which enzymes act on it.
notes.1: Proteases act only on proteins. Starch is a different nutrient, so think about which enzymes act on it.

why.right: Starch needs carbohydrases because starch is a carbohydrate and each enzyme acts on one type of substance.
wrong: Starch needs carbohydrases because carbohydrases can digest every type of food in bread.
Starch needs carbohydrases because starch is a protein that only carbohydrases can break down.

questions.q: A piece of apple has just been swallowed. Which organ is it in now?
questions.explain: After swallowing, food passes from the mouth into the gullet. The gullet carries it down to the stomach.
questions.lo: Place the organs of the digestive system in order

notes.0: The stomach comes after the gullet. Food that has just been swallowed has not reached it yet.
notes.1: The small intestine comes after the stomach. Food that has just been swallowed is still near the mouth.
notes.2: The rectum is near the end of the digestive system. Food that has just been swallowed is still near the mouth.

why.right: Swallowed food is in the gullet because the gullet is the tube joining the mouth to the stomach.
wrong: Swallowed food is in the gullet because the gullet is where food is stored for several hours.
Swallowed food is in the gullet because the gullet is where most digested food is absorbed.

questions.q: Which organ comes directly after the stomach?
questions.explain: Food passes from the stomach directly into the small intestine.
questions.lo: Place the organs of the digestive system in order

notes.1: The gullet comes before the stomach, carrying food from the mouth. Think about where food goes after it leaves the stomach.
notes.2: The rectum is near the end of the system, after the large intestine. Think about where food goes after it leaves the stomach.
notes.3: The large intestine comes later, after the small intestine. Think about the order of the organs after the stomach.

questions.q: Food has just left the large intestine. Where does it go next?
questions.explain: After the large intestine, undigested food passes into the rectum, where faeces is stored. It then leaves the body through the anus.
questions.lo: Place the organs of the digestive system in order

notes.1: The anus is the opening at the very end. Faeces is stored in another part before it leaves through the anus.
notes.2: The small intestine comes before the large intestine. Food does not move backwards.
notes.3: The stomach comes much earlier. Food does not move backwards along the digestive system.

questions.q: Food is now in the small intestine. Where was it just before?
questions.explain: Food passes from the stomach into the small intestine. So just before the small intestine, the food was in the stomach.
questions.lo: Place the organs of the digestive system in order

notes.0: The large intestine comes after the small intestine, not before it. Think about the organ just before the small intestine.
notes.1: The gullet carries food towards the small intestine, but there is one more organ in between. Think about the organ just before the small intestine.
notes.2: The mouth is at the start. The food passes through two more organs before it reaches the small intestine.

questions.q: Besides starting starch digestion, saliva
questions.explain: Saliva contains mucus, which softens and lubricates food so it is easier to swallow. Saliva also contains carbohydrases that start starch digestion.
questions.lo: State the function of each part of the digestive system

notes.0: Harmful microorganisms in food are mainly killed by the acid in the stomach. Think about how saliva helps food go down.
notes.2: Water is absorbed mainly in the large intestine, not by saliva. Think about how saliva helps food go down.
notes.3: Saliva has no proteases, so it does not digest proteins. Think about how saliva helps food go down.

questions.q: What do the muscles of the gullet do?
questions.explain: The muscles in the wall of the gullet contract in waves. This pushes food down towards the stomach.
questions.lo: State the function of each part of the digestive system

notes.0: Gastric juice is released by the stomach, not the gullet. Think about how food travels down the gullet.
notes.1: Churning happens in the stomach. Think about how food travels down the gullet.
notes.3: Digested food is absorbed in the small intestine. Think about how food travels down the gullet.

questions.q: The hydrochloric acid in gastric juice
questions.explain: The hydrochloric acid in gastric juice kills most harmful microorganisms in food. This helps to protect the body from disease.
questions.lo: State the function of each part of the digestive system

notes.0: Fats are digested by lipases, mainly in the small intestine. Acid does not digest fats.
notes.1: Mineral salts are absorbed in the intestines, not by the acid. Think about what a strong acid does to living things in food.
notes.2: Lubricating food is done by mucus in saliva. Think about what a strong acid does to living things in food.

questions.q: What is the function of the mucus lining the stomach?
questions.explain: The stomach wall makes mucus, which forms a layer over its lining. This stops the hydrochloric acid and enzymes from damaging the stomach.
questions.lo: State the function of each part of the digestive system

notes.1: Harmful microorganisms are killed by the hydrochloric acid, not the mucus. Think about what the stomach lining needs protection from.
notes.2: Proteins are digested by proteases in gastric juice, not by mucus. Think about what the stomach lining needs protection from.
notes.3: Digested food is absorbed in the small intestine, not by stomach mucus. Think about what the stomach lining needs protection from.

why.right: Stomach mucus protects the stomach because it forms a layer that keeps acid away from the lining.
wrong: Stomach mucus protects the stomach because it turns the acid into water before it is used.
Stomach mucus protects the stomach because it absorbs the acid and carries it into the blood.

questions.q: Remaining water and mineral salts in food are absorbed in the
questions.explain: The large intestine absorbs the remaining water and mineral salts from undigested food. This leaves semi-solid faeces.
questions.lo: State the function of each part of the digestive system

notes.0: The gullet only carries food to the stomach. Little is absorbed there. Think about the organ that food passes through after the small intestine.
notes.1: The stomach absorbs very little. Think about the organ that food passes through after the small intestine.
notes.3: The rectum stores faeces. Most of the remaining water has been removed before faeces reaches it.

questions.q: Where is faeces stored before it leaves the body?
questions.explain: Faeces is stored in the rectum. It leaves the body through the anus.
questions.lo: State the function of each part of the digestive system

notes.0: The stomach holds food early in digestion. Faeces forms much later, near the end of the system.
notes.2: The large intestine absorbs water to form faeces. Faeces is then stored in the next part before it leaves.
notes.3: The anus is the opening that faeces passes out through. It is not where faeces is stored.

questions.q: The small intestine has many internal folds. This helps it
questions.explain: Internal folds give the small intestine a larger surface area. More digested food can then be absorbed into the blood.
questions.lo: State the function of each part of the digestive system

notes.0: Hydrochloric acid is made in the stomach, not the small intestine. Think about what a larger surface area helps the small intestine do.
notes.1: Churning is done by the stomach. Folds give a larger surface area, so think about what the small intestine does with digested food.
notes.3: Faeces is stored in the rectum. Think about what a larger surface area helps the small intestine do.

why.right: Folds help the small intestine because a larger surface area lets more digested food pass into the blood.
wrong: Folds help the small intestine because they trap food and keep it there for several days.
Folds help the small intestine because they squeeze food hard enough to grind it into pieces.

questions.q: Where does the digestion of starch begin?
questions.explain: Starch digestion begins in the mouth. Saliva contains carbohydrases that start breaking starch into simple sugars.
questions.lo: Identify where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested

notes.0: Starch digestion is completed in the small intestine, but it starts earlier. Think about where food first meets an enzyme.
notes.2: Starch digestion does continue in the gullet, using enzymes released earlier. Think about where those enzymes are released.
notes.3: The stomach has no carbohydrases. Think about where food first meets an enzyme that acts on starch.

why.right: Starch digestion begins in the mouth because saliva contains carbohydrases that act on starch.
wrong: Starch digestion begins in the mouth because teeth break starch into simple sugars.
Starch digestion begins in the mouth because saliva contains proteases that act on starch.

questions.q: Where does the digestion of proteins begin?
questions.explain: Protein digestion begins in the stomach. Gastric juice contains proteases that start breaking proteins down.
questions.lo: Identify where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested

notes.1: Saliva contains carbohydrases but no proteases. Think about where food first meets an enzyme that acts on protein.
notes.2: Protein digestion is completed in the small intestine, but it starts earlier. Think about where food first meets an enzyme that acts on protein.
notes.3: The gullet makes no digestive enzymes. Think about where food first meets an enzyme that acts on protein.

why.right: Protein digestion begins in the stomach because gastric juice contains proteases that act on proteins.
wrong: Protein digestion begins in the stomach because the hydrochloric acid digests proteins on its own.
Protein digestion begins in the stomach because gastric juice contains lipases that act on proteins.

questions.q: Where does the digestion of fats begin?
questions.explain: Fat digestion begins in the small intestine. This is where lipases are first released onto the food.
questions.lo: Identify where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested

notes.0: The stomach's gastric juice acts mainly on proteins. Think about where food first meets lipases.
notes.1: The large intestine absorbs water. Digestion is complete before food reaches it.
notes.2: Saliva contains carbohydrases, not lipases. Think about where food first meets lipases.

why.right: Fat digestion begins in the small intestine because that is where lipases first act on the food.
wrong: Fat digestion begins in the small intestine because fats cannot pass through the stomach.
Fat digestion begins in the small intestine because the acid there breaks fats into fatty acids.

questions.q: Where are carbohydrates, proteins and fats all fully digested?
questions.explain: The small intestine contains carbohydrases, proteases and lipases. Digestion of all three nutrients is completed there.
questions.lo: Identify where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested

notes.0: The stomach digests mainly proteins. It does not complete the digestion of carbohydrates and fats.
notes.1: The mouth only starts the digestion of starch. Think about where enzymes for all three nutrients act.
notes.3: The large intestine absorbs water and mineral salts. Digestion is complete before food reaches it.

why.right: All three nutrients are fully digested in the small intestine because it has enzymes for each of them.
wrong: All three nutrients are fully digested in the small intestine because its acid breaks down every nutrient.
All three nutrients are fully digested in the small intestine because one enzyme there acts on all foods.

questions.q: A boy eats a fried egg. Where does digestion of its fat begin?
questions.explain: Fat digestion begins in the small intestine, where lipases act on fats. The fat in the egg passes through the mouth, gullet and stomach before lipases act on it.
questions.lo: Identify where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested

notes.0: Saliva has carbohydrases, not lipases, so fat is not digested in the mouth. Think about where food first meets lipases.
notes.1: The stomach mainly digests proteins. Think about where food first meets lipases.
notes.2: The gullet makes no digestive enzymes. Think about where food first meets lipases.

why.right: Fat in an egg starts to be digested in the small intestine because lipases are first found there.
wrong: Fat in an egg starts to be digested in the small intestine because teeth cannot crush fat into pieces.
Fat in an egg starts to be digested in the small intestine because stomach acid turns the fat into protein.

questions.q: Starch is still digested in the gullet. Why?
choices: carbohydrases from saliva are mixed with food
gastric juice flows into the gullet
questions.explain: Saliva is mixed with food in the mouth. Its carbohydrases travel down with the food and keep digesting starch in the gullet.
questions.lo: Identify where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested

notes.0: The gullet makes no digestive enzymes. Think about where the enzymes in the swallowed food came from.
notes.2: The gullet does not churn food. It pushes food along. Churning is also physical, so it would not digest starch molecules.
notes.3: Gastric juice stays in the stomach and does not flow up into the gullet. Think about where the enzymes in the swallowed food came from.

why.right: Starch is still digested in the gullet because enzymes from saliva travel down with the food.
wrong: Starch is still digested in the gullet because the gullet wall releases its own carbohydrases.
Starch is still digested in the gullet because gastric juice flows upward from the stomach.

questions.q: A boy drinks orange juice containing fibre. What happens to the fibre?
choices: it forms part of the faeces
it is digested into simple sugars
it is absorbed in the stomach
questions.explain: Humans have no enzymes that digest fibre. Fibre passes through the system undigested and forms part of the faeces.
questions.lo: Identify where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested

notes.1: Humans do not have enzymes that break down fibre. Think about what happens to food that cannot be digested.
notes.2: Fibre is not absorbed anywhere in the digestive system. Think about what happens to food that cannot be digested.
notes.3: Lipases act only on fats, and fibre is not a fat. Think about what happens to food that cannot be digested.

why.right: Fibre ends up in faeces because the human body has no enzymes that can digest it.
wrong: Fibre ends up in faeces because it is digested into simple sugars that the body cannot use.
Fibre ends up in faeces because it is absorbed into the blood and then removed.

questions.q: Why is the digestive system made up of several organs?
choices: no single organ can complete digestion
food is digested only in the mouth
the stomach can digest all food alone
questions.explain: Each organ does a different part of digestion, with different enzymes and conditions. No single organ can complete digestion, so several organs work together.
questions.lo: Explain why the organs must work together to digest food

notes.1: Each organ has different enzymes and digests only some nutrients. Think about whether one organ alone could finish the job.
notes.2: Digestion also happens in the stomach and small intestine. Think about whether one organ alone could finish the job.
notes.3: The stomach mainly digests proteins and cannot digest all food alone. Think about whether one organ could finish the job.

why.right: Digestion needs several organs because each organ carries out only part of the process with its own enzymes.
wrong: Digestion needs several organs because each organ digests every nutrient a little at a time.
Digestion needs several organs because food must be stored in each organ for a whole day.

questions.q: Cells use simple sugars to
questions.explain: Cells use simple sugars such as glucose in respiration. Respiration releases the energy that cells need.
questions.lo: State that end products are used for respiration, growth and tissue repair

notes.0: Repairing damaged tissues uses amino acids from proteins. Think about what cells release from simple sugars to stay active.
notes.2: Faeces is made of undigested food, not of absorbed sugars. Think about what cells release from simple sugars to stay active.
notes.3: In this chapter, fats in the body are made from fatty acids and glycerol. Think about what cells release from simple sugars to stay active.

questions.q: Amino acids are used by the body for
questions.explain: Amino acids are used to make new proteins. These proteins are needed for cell growth and to repair damaged tissues.
questions.lo: State that end products are used for respiration, growth and tissue repair

notes.0: Faeces is made of undigested food, not of absorbed amino acids. Think about what the body builds from amino acids.
notes.1: Fats in the body are made from fatty acids and glycerol. Think about what the body builds from amino acids.
notes.2: Microorganisms in food are killed mainly by stomach acid. Think about what the body builds from amino acids.

questions.q: Fatty acids and glycerol are used to
questions.explain: Fatty acids and glycerol are joined together again in the body to make fats, which are stored.
questions.lo: State that end products are used for respiration, growth and tissue repair

notes.0: Repairing damaged tissues uses amino acids. Think about what fatty acids and glycerol can be joined back into.
notes.1: Microorganisms are killed mainly by stomach acid. Think about what fatty acids and glycerol can be joined back into.
notes.3: Simple sugars come from digested carbohydrates. Think about what fatty acids and glycerol can be joined back into.

questions.q: An athlete is recovering from a muscle injury. Which nutrient helps repair most?
questions.explain: Proteins are digested into amino acids. The body uses amino acids for cell growth and to repair damaged tissues such as injured muscle.
questions.lo: State that end products are used for respiration, growth and tissue repair

notes.0: Fibre is not digested and is not used for building tissue. Think about which nutrient gives the body amino acids.
notes.1: Carbohydrates mainly supply energy. Think about which nutrient gives the body the building blocks for repair.
notes.3: Fats mainly store energy. Think about which nutrient gives the body the building blocks for repair.

why.right: Proteins help repair muscle because they are digested into amino acids that build new cells.
wrong: Proteins help repair muscle because they are digested into simple sugars that build new cells.
Proteins help repair muscle because they pass into the muscle without being digested first.

questions.q: A runner needs energy quickly. Which end product do her cells use?
questions.explain: Cells use simple sugars in respiration to release energy. Simple sugars are the quickest source of energy for the runner's cells.
questions.lo: State that end products are used for respiration, growth and tissue repair

notes.0: Amino acids are used mainly for growth and repair. Think about which end product cells use first for respiration.
notes.2: Glycerol is used with fatty acids to make fats for storage. Think about which end product cells use first for respiration.
notes.3: Fatty acids are used mainly to make fats for storage. Think about which end product cells use first for respiration.

why.right: A runner's cells use simple sugars for quick energy because sugars release energy readily in respiration.
wrong: A runner's cells use simple sugars for quick energy because sugars are used to build new muscle.
A runner's cells use simple sugars for quick energy because sugars give energy without respiration.

questions.q: Diabetes is a disease in which the blood sugar level is
questions.explain: Diabetes is a disease in which the blood sugar level is too high because the body cannot control it properly.
questions.lo: Describe diabetes and the food and lifestyle choices that reduce its risk

notes.0: If the blood sugar level were always normal, there would be no disease. Diabetes is a problem with controlling blood sugar.
notes.1: Blood always contains some sugar while a person is alive. Think about whether the level in diabetes is above or below normal.
notes.2: A blood sugar level that is too low is a different problem. Think about whether the level in diabetes is above or below normal.

questions.q: What does insulin do?
choices: keeps the blood sugar level balanced
questions.explain: Insulin is a hormone that keeps the blood sugar level balanced. It lowers the blood sugar level when it rises too high.
questions.lo: Describe diabetes and the food and lifestyle choices that reduce its risk

notes.1: Insulin is not a digestive enzyme, and simple sugars are already digested. Think about what insulin does to the amount of sugar in the blood.
notes.2: Fats are broken down by lipases, not insulin. Think about what insulin does to the amount of sugar in the blood.
notes.3: Insulin does not kill bacteria. Think about what insulin does to the amount of sugar in the blood.

questions.q: Which is a common symptom of diabetes?
questions.explain: In diabetes the kidneys remove extra sugar from the blood in urine, which takes a lot of water with it. This causes frequent urination.
questions.lo: Describe diabetes and the food and lifestyle choices that reduce its risk

notes.0: In diabetes, wounds heal slowly, not quickly. Think about how the body tries to get rid of extra sugar in the blood.
notes.2: Diabetes often causes weight loss, not sudden weight gain. Think about how the body tries to get rid of extra sugar in the blood.
notes.3: People with diabetes often feel more hungry, not less. Think about how the body tries to get rid of extra sugar in the blood.

why.right: Diabetes causes frequent urination because the kidneys remove the extra blood sugar with a lot of water.
wrong: Diabetes causes frequent urination because the extra blood sugar makes a person drink less water.
Diabetes causes frequent urination because insulin turns the extra blood sugar into urine.

questions.q: Which choice lowers the risk of diabetes?
choices: exercising 30 minutes, five days a week
questions.explain: Regular exercise helps the body use up sugar and keeps body mass healthy. This lowers the risk of diabetes.
questions.lo: Describe diabetes and the food and lifestyle choices that reduce its risk

notes.1: Fried food is high in fat and can lead to weight gain, which raises the risk of diabetes. Think about habits that keep body mass healthy.
notes.2: Health screenings help find diabetes early. Skipping them does not lower the risk. Think about habits that keep body mass healthy.
notes.3: Sugary drinks raise the blood sugar level and can lead to weight gain. Think about habits that keep body mass healthy.

why.right: Regular exercise lowers the risk of diabetes because it helps the body use up sugar and stay at a healthy mass.
wrong: Regular exercise lowers the risk of diabetes because it makes the body produce no sugar at all.
Regular exercise lowers the risk of diabetes because it removes all the sugar from the blood through sweat.

questions.q: Prediabetes has no symptoms. How can it be detected?
questions.explain: Prediabetes is a blood sugar level that is higher than normal but not high enough to be diabetes. It can only be found by checking the blood sugar level.
questions.lo: Describe diabetes and the food and lifestyle choices that reduce its risk

notes.0: Counting heartbeats does not show the amount of sugar in the blood. Prediabetes is about the blood sugar level.
notes.1: Prediabetes has no symptoms, so waiting for weight loss would not detect it. Think about measuring what is actually raised.
notes.2: Blurred vision is a symptom, and prediabetes has no symptoms. Think about measuring what is actually raised.

why.right: Prediabetes is found by a blood test because its only sign is a blood sugar level above normal.
wrong: Prediabetes is found by a blood test because the blood turns a different colour when sugar is high.
Prediabetes is found by a blood test because it always causes blurred vision before anything else.

questions.q: In constipation, faeces is hard and dry because
choices: too little water is absorbed from it
too much water is absorbed from it
questions.explain: In constipation, faeces stays in the large intestine for too long. Too much water is absorbed from it, so it becomes hard and dry.
questions.lo: Identify causes and prevention of constipation, gastritis and food poisoning

notes.0: If too little water were absorbed, the faeces would be watery, as in diarrhoea. Think about what makes faeces dry.
notes.1: Faeces that moves too quickly has less time for water to be absorbed, so it is watery. Think about what makes faeces dry.
notes.3: Acid is made in the stomach and does not dry out faeces. Think about what the large intestine takes out of faeces.

why.right: Faeces in constipation is hard because it stays too long in the large intestine and loses too much water.
wrong: Faeces in constipation is hard because the stomach adds extra acid that sets it solid in the intestine.
Faeces in constipation is hard because the large intestine adds extra fibre to it as it passes.

questions.q: Gastritis is the inflammation of the
questions.explain: Gastritis is the inflammation of the stomach lining. It can be caused by too much acid, skipping meals or certain bacteria.
questions.lo: Identify causes and prevention of constipation, gastritis and food poisoning

notes.0: The large intestine is linked to problems such as constipation. Gastritis comes from the word gastric, as in gastric juice. Think about where that is made.
notes.2: The rectum stores faeces. Gastritis comes from the word gastric, as in gastric juice. Think about where that is made.
notes.3: The gullet carries food down to the next organ. Gastritis comes from the word gastric, as in gastric juice. Think about where that is made.

questions.q: Which habit helps prevent constipation?
questions.explain: Fibre adds bulk to faeces and helps it hold water. This keeps faeces soft and helps it move along the large intestine.
questions.lo: Identify causes and prevention of constipation, gastritis and food poisoning

notes.0: Skipping meals does not help faeces move. It raises the risk of gastritis. Think about what keeps faeces soft and bulky.
notes.1: Oily food is low in fibre and does not help faeces move. Think about what keeps faeces soft and bulky.
notes.3: Drinking less water makes faeces harder and drier. Think about what keeps faeces soft and bulky.

why.right: A high-fibre diet prevents constipation because fibre adds bulk and keeps faeces soft so it moves easily.
wrong: A high-fibre diet prevents constipation because fibre is digested into water in the large intestine.
A high-fibre diet prevents constipation because fibre makes the large intestine absorb more water.

questions.q: Which habit increases the risk of gastritis?
questions.explain: Skipping meals leaves the stomach empty while it still makes acid. The acid can irritate the stomach lining and lead to gastritis.
questions.lo: Identify causes and prevention of constipation, gastritis and food poisoning

notes.0: Drinking more water does not harm the stomach lining. Think about what happens when the stomach makes acid but has no food in it.
notes.1: High-fibre food helps prevent constipation and does not harm the stomach lining. Think about what happens when the stomach is empty.
notes.2: Regular exercise is a healthy habit and does not harm the stomach lining. Think about what happens when the stomach is empty.

why.right: Skipping meals raises the risk of gastritis because stomach acid can attack the lining when there is no food.
wrong: Skipping meals raises the risk of gastritis because the stomach lining dries out when there is no food.
Skipping meals raises the risk of gastritis because the empty stomach absorbs its own acid into the blood.

questions.q: A girl rarely drinks water and passes hard, dry faeces. Which issue is this?
questions.explain: Hard, dry faeces is the main sign of constipation. Drinking too little water makes this more likely.
questions.lo: Identify causes and prevention of constipation, gastritis and food poisoning

notes.1: Diabetes is about a high blood sugar level, not about faeces. Think about which issue causes hard, dry faeces.
notes.2: Food poisoning usually causes diarrhoea and vomiting, not hard, dry faeces. Think about which issue causes hard, dry faeces.
notes.3: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining and causes stomach pain. Think about which issue causes hard, dry faeces.

why.right: Hard, dry faeces points to constipation because the large intestine has removed too much water from the faeces.
wrong: Hard, dry faeces points to constipation because the blood sugar level in the body is too high.
Hard, dry faeces points to constipation because the stomach lining has been inflamed by acid.

questions.q: A man has diarrhoea and vomiting after eating spoilt food. Which issue is this?
questions.explain: Spoilt food can contain harmful bacteria or their poisons. Eating it causes food poisoning, with diarrhoea and vomiting.
questions.lo: Identify causes and prevention of constipation, gastritis and food poisoning

notes.0: Diabetes is about a high blood sugar level and does not come from one meal. Think about what spoilt food can contain.
notes.2: Constipation causes hard, dry faeces, not diarrhoea. Think about what spoilt food can contain.
notes.3: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining, often from acid. Think about what spoilt food can contain.

why.right: Spoilt food causes food poisoning because it can contain harmful bacteria or poisons made by them.
wrong: Spoilt food causes food poisoning because it has lost all of its nutrients and fibre.
Spoilt food causes food poisoning because it raises the blood sugar level very quickly.

questions.q: Raw food in a refrigerator should be kept below
questions.explain: Raw food in a refrigerator should be kept below 5 °C. At this temperature harmful bacteria grow very slowly, so the food stays safe for longer.
questions.lo: Apply food safety tips for handling and choosing food

notes.0: 25 °C is about room temperature, and bacteria grow quickly at this temperature. A refrigerator needs to be much colder.
notes.1: At 10 °C bacteria can still grow quite quickly. A refrigerator needs to be colder than this to keep raw food safe.
notes.3: 18 °C is a warm temperature where bacteria grow quickly. The freezer value of minus 18 °C is a different thing.

why.right: Raw food in a refrigerator is kept below 5 °C because bacteria grow very slowly at such low temperatures.
wrong: Raw food in a refrigerator is kept below 5 °C because all bacteria are killed at such low temperatures.
Raw food in a refrigerator is kept below 5 °C because the food freezes solid at such low temperatures.

questions.q: Frozen food should be stored below
questions.explain: Frozen food should be stored below −18 °C. At this temperature bacteria cannot grow, so the food stays safe for a long time.
questions.lo: Apply food safety tips for handling and choosing food

notes.0: 4 °C is a refrigerator temperature. Frozen food needs to be stored much colder than this.
notes.1: Minus 5 °C is not cold enough for safe long-term storage of frozen food. It needs to be much colder than this.
notes.2: 0 °C is only the freezing point of water. Frozen food needs to be stored much colder than this.

why.right: Frozen food is stored below −18 °C because bacteria cannot grow at such low temperatures.
wrong: Frozen food is stored below −18 °C because all bacteria are killed at such low temperatures.
Frozen food is stored below −18 °C because water in food only freezes at this temperature.

questions.q: Where should cooked food be placed in a refrigerator?
questions.explain: Cooked food should be placed above raw food. Juices from raw food can drip down and carry harmful bacteria onto any food below it.
questions.lo: Apply food safety tips for handling and choosing food

notes.1: Leaving cooked food uncovered next to raw food lets bacteria spread between them. Think about where juices from raw food can drip.
notes.2: Juices from raw food can drip onto anything below it. Think about where the cooked food would be safe from drips.
notes.3: Touching lets bacteria pass directly from raw food to cooked food. Think about where cooked food is safe from raw food.

why.right: Cooked food goes above raw food because juices from raw food can drip bacteria onto food below.
wrong: Cooked food goes above raw food because warm air rises and keeps the cooked food hot.
Cooked food goes above raw food because cooked food is heavier and could crush the raw food.

questions.q: A shop keeps frozen fish at −5 °C. Should you buy it?
choices: no, because it is too cold
yes, because frozen food cannot spoil
no, because it is not cold enough
questions.explain: Frozen food should be stored below −18 °C. At −5 °C the fish is not cold enough to stop bacteria growing, so it should not be bought.
questions.lo: Apply food safety tips for handling and choosing food

notes.0: Frozen food cannot be too cold for safety. Compare −5 °C with the temperature frozen food should be stored below.
notes.1: Frozen food can still spoil if it is not kept cold enough. Compare −5 °C with the temperature frozen food should be stored below.
notes.3: Being below 0 °C is not enough. Compare −5 °C with the temperature frozen food should be stored below.

why.right: Fish at −5 °C is unsafe to buy because frozen food must be kept below −18 °C to stop bacteria growing.
wrong: Fish at −5 °C is unsafe to buy because any temperature below 0 °C destroys the nutrients in fish.
Fish at −5 °C is unsafe to buy because frozen food must be kept above 0 °C to stay fresh.

questions.q: Which can of food should not be eaten?
choices: a can within its expiry date
a can stored in a cool place
questions.explain: A badly dented can may have a damaged seal. Air and bacteria can get in, so the food inside may be unsafe to eat.
questions.lo: Apply food safety tips for handling and choosing food

notes.0: A tightly sealed can keeps air and bacteria out, so the food is safe. Look for a can whose seal may be damaged.
notes.1: A can within its expiry date is safe if it is undamaged. Look for a can whose seal may be damaged.
notes.2: Storing cans in a cool place is correct. Look for a can whose seal may be damaged.

why.right: A badly dented can is unsafe because its seal may be broken, letting bacteria into the food.
wrong: A badly dented can is unsafe because the metal at the dent dissolves into the food at once.
A badly dented can is unsafe because the dent makes the food go past its expiry date.

questions.q: Most bacteria in our digestive system are
questions.explain: Most bacteria in the digestive system are beneficial. They help digest some food and produce certain vitamins. Only a few types are harmful.
questions.lo: Classify effects of bacteria in the digestive system as beneficial or harmful

notes.1: Many bacteria live in the gut all the time, not only in food. Think about what most of these gut bacteria do for us.
notes.2: Some gut bacteria are harmful, but they are only a few types. Think about what most gut bacteria do for us.
notes.3: Most gut bacteria are not deadly. Many of them help with digestion. Think about what most gut bacteria do for us.

questions.q: Which food is produced using bacteria?
questions.explain: Yoghurt is made by adding bacteria to milk. The bacteria change the milk, making it thicker and sour.
questions.lo: Classify effects of bacteria in the digestive system as beneficial or harmful

notes.0: Plain rice is cooked in water and is not made using bacteria. Think about a food made by changing milk.
notes.2: A fresh apple grows on a tree and is not made using bacteria. Think about a food made by changing milk.
notes.3: A boiled egg is only cooked in hot water. Think about a food made by changing milk.

questions.q: Gut bacteria help us digest some carbohydrates. This effect is
questions.explain: Gut bacteria help us digest some carbohydrates that our own enzymes cannot break down. This helps the body, so the effect is beneficial.
questions.lo: Classify effects of bacteria in the digestive system as beneficial or harmful

notes.0: Helping digestion does affect the body. Think about whether this effect helps or harms us.
notes.1: A harmful effect damages the body, as in a stomach ulcer. Think about whether helping digestion helps or harms us.

why.right: Gut bacteria that aid digestion are beneficial because they help break down food our enzymes cannot.
wrong: Gut bacteria that aid digestion are beneficial because they kill all the other bacteria in the gut.
Gut bacteria that aid digestion are beneficial because they stop the stomach from making any acid.

questions.q: Which is a harmful effect of bacteria?
questions.explain: Some bacteria can infect the stomach lining and cause a stomach ulcer. This is a harmful effect. The other options are beneficial effects of gut bacteria.
questions.lo: Classify effects of bacteria in the digestive system as beneficial or harmful

notes.0: Helping to absorb mineral salts is good for the body. Look for an effect that damages the body.
notes.1: Helping to digest some food is good for the body. Look for an effect that damages the body.
notes.2: Producing certain vitamins is good for the body. Look for an effect that damages the body.

questions.q: Carbohydrase is added to starch and to protein. Only starch is digested. Enzymes are
questions.explain: The carbohydrase digested the starch but not the protein. This shows that enzymes are specific. Each enzyme acts on only one type of substance.
questions.lo: Interpret an investigation of the effect of enzymes on food

notes.1: The result shows which substance was digested, not whether the enzyme was used up. Think about why the protein was left unchanged.
notes.2: The protein was not digested, so the enzyme cannot digest all food. Think about why the protein was left unchanged.
notes.3: Carbohydrases are also made in the small intestine, and this test was done in tubes. Think about why the protein was left unchanged.

why.right: This result shows enzymes are specific because the carbohydrase acted on starch but not on protein.
wrong: This result shows enzymes are specific because the carbohydrase was used up by the starch.
This result shows enzymes are specific because the carbohydrase only works inside the mouth.

questions.q: Protease is added to egg white in one tube and water to another. The water tube is the
questions.explain: The water tube has no protease. It shows what happens without the enzyme, so it is the control for comparison.
questions.lo: Interpret an investigation of the effect of enzymes on food

notes.0: The variable measured is the result recorded, such as how much egg white is digested. The water tube is set up for comparison.
notes.2: A conclusion is a statement made after the results are seen. The water tube is a test tube set up for comparison.
notes.3: A hypothesis is a prediction made before the experiment. The water tube is a test tube set up for comparison.

why.right: The water tube is the control because it shows what happens to egg white without any protease.
wrong: The water tube is the control because water digests egg white faster than protease does.
The water tube is the control because water is the enzyme being tested in the experiment.

questions.q: A student tests how temperature affects protease action. Which is the variable changed?
questions.explain: The student is testing how temperature affects protease action. So temperature is the variable that is changed on purpose.
questions.lo: Interpret an investigation of the effect of enzymes on food

notes.0: The mass of egg white should be kept the same in every test so the test is fair. Look at what the student is testing the effect of.
notes.1: The volume of protease should be kept the same in every test so the test is fair. Look at what the student is testing the effect of.
notes.2: The time taken to digest protein is what is measured as the result. Look at what the student is testing the effect of.

why.right: Temperature is the variable changed because the student wants to find out how it affects protease action.
wrong: Temperature is the variable changed because it is the result that the student measures at the end.
Temperature is the variable changed because it must be kept the same for a fair test.

questions.q: A detergent removes oil stains from clothes. Which enzyme does it contain?
questions.explain: Oil is a type of fat. Lipases break down fats, so a detergent that removes oil stains contains lipases.
questions.lo: Interpret an investigation of the effect of enzymes on food

notes.1: Proteases break down proteins, such as egg or blood stains. Think about what type of nutrient oil is.
notes.2: Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates such as starch. Think about what type of nutrient oil is.

why.right: Detergents for oil stains contain lipases because oil is a fat and lipases act only on fats.
wrong: Detergents for oil stains contain lipases because lipases can break down every type of stain.
Detergents for oil stains contain lipases because oil is a protein that lipases break down.
